headline: Europe’s wildfires ignite buried World War bombs, turning forests into minefields
deck: As record fires scour the continent, dormant ordnance from the 20th century’s bloodiest conflicts is detonating across former battlefields, forcing authorities to deploy driverless tanks in an unprecedented firefighting experiment.
body: Wildfires in Europe are detonating tens of thousands of buried bombs and mines from World War I and World War II, transforming charred landscapes into instant minefields. The blasts are forcing evacuations, halting firefighting operations, and killing emergency responders caught in the crossfire. In France alone, authorities report at least three firefighters injured by secondary explosions in the past month. The phenomenon is not isolated: reports from Spain, Italy, and Greece confirm similar incidents as fires expose decades-old ordnance. For residents near former frontlines, the fires have turned their backyards into deathtraps.

Unexploded ordnance from the two world wars has long plagued Europe, lurking beneath farmland and construction sites in former frontline regions. But the scale of the current crisis is unprecedented. Firefighters battling record-breaking wildfires are now encountering live ammunition, artillery shells, and anti-personnel mines erupting from the earth as flames consume the topsoil. The problem is worst in areas where the Western Front once stretched from the North Sea to Switzerland, or where partisan resistance fighters left caches of explosives in the rugged terrain of the Balkans. What was once a slow-burn hazard is now an immediate, explosive threat.

The detonations are directly linked to the intensity of the fires. As wildfires burn hotter and deeper than in past decades, they are unearthing ordnance buried for generations. In Greece, a firefighter was killed last week when a shell exploded mid-operation, underscoring the lethal synergy between climate change and wartime relics. Authorities in Spain’s Catalonia region have warned residents not to approach smoldering areas, as buried TNT and white phosphorus can reignite days or even weeks after the initial blaze. The situation has forced a grim calculus: evacuate now, or risk encountering ordnance later.

To combat the dual threat of fire and explosives, some countries are turning to unorthodox solutions. The Wall Street Journal reports that firefighting teams in Italy and France are deploying driverless tanks equipped with water cannons to douse flames in areas contaminated by World War II ammunition. These remote-controlled vehicles allow crews to extinguish fires without risking human lives in mine-pocked terrain. The tactic marks a stark departure from traditional firefighting, blending 21st-century robotics with 20th-century ordnance. Yet even this technology has limits; the tanks cannot operate in terrain too unstable for their treads, leaving some areas to burn uncontrollably.

The crisis is a brutal reminder of Europe’s unfinished business with its past. Decades after the guns fell silent, the continent remains littered with an estimated 100,000 tons of unexploded ordnance, according to declassified military records. In Belgium, bomb disposal teams recover over 300 tons of munitions annually from construction sites and farm fields. The wildfires have accelerated this grim harvest, turning forests into active conflict zones. In one Italian village, residents were forced to shelter in place for 48 hours after a wildfire triggered a chain reaction of detonations, shattering windows and collapsing roofs.

The human toll is mounting. In Greece, a family of four was airlifted to safety after their home was damaged by a secondary explosion triggered by a passing wildfire. In Slovenia, a farmer lost his leg when he accidentally struck a buried anti-tank mine while surveying storm damage. These incidents highlight the broader risks: not just to those fleeing fires, but to anyone living or working in areas once ravaged by war. Emergency services are stretched thin, with bomb disposal units now embedded in firefighting teams—a logistical nightmare that slows response times and increases costs. The European Union has pledged additional funding for ordnance clearance, but the scale of the problem dwarfs available resources.

Experts warn that the problem will only worsen as climate change intensifies wildfire seasons. A 2023 study by the European Environment Agency found that the number of high-risk fire days has doubled since 1980, with the trend expected to continue. The same areas burning today are likely to burn hotter and longer in the future, exposing more ordnance and creating a feedback loop of danger. Meanwhile, aging munitions—some corroded, others filled with unstable explosives—are increasingly prone to accidental detonation. The European Commission has called for a continent-wide mapping effort to identify high-risk zones, but progress has been slow.

The driverless tanks offer a temporary fix, but they underscore a larger failure: Europe’s inability to fully address its wartime legacy. Countries like Germany and France have poured billions into bomb disposal programs, yet the wildfires have exposed glaring gaps. In Poland, a 2022 report found that 12% of the country’s territory remains contaminated with unexploded ordnance, with clearance efforts projected to take another 30 years. The current crisis makes one thing clear: the past is not just buried in the ground. It is burning, and it is killing.

For now, authorities are urging caution. Firefighters in Portugal have begun using drones equipped with infrared cameras to scan for heat signatures of buried ordnance before deploying crews. In Austria, the military has been called in to assist with bomb disposal in fire-affected regions, a rare assignment for troops more accustomed to peacekeeping. But the message is the same everywhere: the wildfires are not just a natural disaster. They are a historical detonation, a reminder that Europe’s wars never truly ended—they just went underground.

The explosions are a deadly twist in Europe’s climate emergency. As temperatures rise and droughts deepen, the continent’s forests are transforming from carbon sinks into time bombs. The buried relics of the 20th century’s conflicts are no longer dormant; they are active, unpredictable, and deadly. For the millions of Europeans living in the shadow of past wars, the fires have turned the present into a minefield. And there is no clear path forward—only the slow, dangerous work of defusing the past before it ignites the future.
